predict.q: If you make a pendulum’s string twice as long, what happens to the time for one swing?
options: It takes about 1.4 times as long
predict.reveal: It takes about **1.4 times** as long. Swing time grows with the *square root* of the length, so doubling the length multiplies it by √2.

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the swing time growing more slowly than the length when you drag the length slider.
interactive.title: Length and swing time
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: The time for one full swing is T = 2π√(L/g). L is the length of the string and g is the pull of gravity at Earth’s surface.[^2]
interactive.ignores: Air resistance, the weight of the string, and wide swings (more than about 20°), where the simple rule starts to drift.

explain.text:
A pendulum’s [[period]] is the time it takes to swing out and back once. It depends on just two things: the length of the string and the pull of [[gravity]].[^2]

Longer strings swing more slowly, but not in step. The period grows with the *square root* of the length, so four times the length only doubles the swing time.

How far you pull it back barely matters for small swings,[^1] which is why a pendulum makes such a steady clock.

analogy.text: A pendulum is like a child on a swing: a longer rope gives a slower, lazier rhythm, however hard you push.
analogy.breaks: Push a real swing very high and its rhythm does slow down. The simple rule only holds for small swings.

say.prompt: In your own words: why does a longer pendulum swing more slowly, and why doesn’t the size of the swing matter much?
rubric: A longer string means a longer swing time
Swing time grows with the square root of length, not in proportion
For small swings, the size of the swing barely changes the time
say.model: A longer pendulum has further to travel along its arc while gravity pulls on it just as hard, so each swing takes longer. The time grows with the square root of the length: four times as long only doubles it. A bigger swing means more distance but also more speed, and for small swings the two cancel out.

checks.q: A 1 m pendulum takes 2 s per swing. About how long does a 4 m pendulum take?
checks.why: Four times the length gives √4 = 2 times the period: 4 s.

misconception.2: You'd be right if swing time grew in step with length, but it grows with the square root.

sources.quote: For small swings the period of a simple pendulum is approximately independent of the amplitude.
